titleStmt.title: HIART-MCS: High Resilience and Approximated Computing Architecture for Imprecise Mixed-Criticality Systems

analytic.title: HIART-MCS: High Resilience and Approximated Computing Architecture for Imprecise Mixed-Criticality Systems

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: In mixed-criticality systems (MCSs), less-critical tasks are often terminated to ensure the correct execution of high critical tasks. This strategy could however lead to safety hazards, and largely reduce system functionality due to the absence of the discarded tasks. To overcome this problem, we introduce a high resilience and approximated computing framework for MCS, i.e., HIART-MCS. HIART-MCS introduces a novel processor which supports approximation at the hardware level. Associated with this, we also introduce a new intermediate system mode which allows less-critical tasks to be executed with reduced precision instead of being directly dropped out. Corresponding to the HIART-MCS, we further present a new theoretical model and schedulability analysis providing a timing guarantee for the system, followed by optimisations of the mode switch strategy. As demonstrated in both the theoretical and practical evaluations, HIART-MCS effectively improves the survivability of less-critical tasks with limited sacrifice of the critical tasks and negligible extra overhead. It is notable that HIART-MCS is the first practical framework for imprecise MCSs.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: Safety-critical systems have stringent assurance and verification requirements that are absolutely essential to life-critical applications, including medical, automotive, aerospace and industrial automation [1]- [7]. In safety-critical systems, integrating components with different levels of criticalities, e.g., Automotive Safety and Integrity Levels (ASILs) in ISO26262 [8], onto a shared hardware platform has become increasingly important [9], as a result of the diverse functionalities required by modern safety-critical systems (e.g., automated driving [8], [10]) and the rapid evolution of underlying platforms [1]. Such systems are termed Mixed-Criticality Systems (MCS)s [11].

In a dual-criticality MCS,which has two criticality levels (HI and LO), a widely studied theoretical model assumes that the Worst-Case Execution Time (WCET) of a task is estimated with different levels of confidence [2], [11]- [18]. The high-critical WCET (HI-WCET, denoted as C HI i ) has a high level of confidence, but is extremely pessimistic (obtained by static timing analysis, for example). However, the lowcritical WCET (LO-WCET, denoted as C LO i ) is much less pessimistic, but has a relatively lower level of confidence (obtained by experimental measurements, for example) [11]. In general, a high-critical task (HI-task) will be developed and * Corresponding author verified using more rigorous procedures than a low-critical task (LO-task). Therefore, a HI-task has both HI-and LO-WECTs, whereas, a LO-task only has a LO-WCET [8], [11].

To provide a dynamic balance between performance and predictability, conventional MCS models usually have two system modes [11], [19], [20], low-critical mode (LO-mode) and high-critical mode (HI-mode). The system first initialises in LO-mode, where the scheduling policy assumes the execution time of each task does not exceed its LO-WCET. If this assumption is violated, the system switches into HI-mode, where the scheduling policy assumes the execution time of HI- tasks may exceed their LO-WCETs, but will not exceed their HI-WCETs (i.e., LO-tasks are dropped) [21]- [24]. Based on this theoretical model, a number of practical MCS frameworks have been developed, including Richard et al. [25], Gadepalli et al. [26], and Kim et al. [27] Imprecise MCS. As reported by Burns et al. [28] and Baruah et al. [29], terminating the services of LO-tasks in HI-mode can lead to safety hazards, as the system may still rely on the calculation results from a LO-task. Alternatively, we can keep these LO-tasks as much as possible if they do not violated the schedulability of HI-tasks. The LO-tasks in modern MCSs heavily rely on Floating Point (FP) calculations, including Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) [30], image processing [31], and signal processing [32]. Different from the other processor operations (e.g., integer calculations), the FP calculations consume significantly more clock cycles (evidenced in Sec. II-A), which dominate the tasks' computation time.

Approximation is an effective method to reduce the time consumption of FP calculations. That is, the processor cuts down the valid bit-width of FP operands and reduces certain levels of computation precision. With this in mind, we propose a high resilience and approximating computing architecture for MCS, named HIART-MCS. Rather than directly dropping LO- tasks when a HI-task overruns, the HIART-MCS executes the LO-tasks as long as possible with a degree of approximation, achieving a graceful degradation and extending the "life cycle" of LO-tasks. We also recognise the HIART-MCS as an imprecise MCS (IMCS) framework [33]- [36]. To achieve this, we propose

• A novel processor (the HIART-processor) to support approximation at the hardware level. • A new intermediate system mode (MID-mode) to the conventional dual-mode MCS model. In MID-mode, HIARTprocessor can execute tasks using approximation. • An experiment-based method to determine a suitable degree of approximation for each LO-task and its corresponding WCET in MID-mode. • A new system architecture and a mode switch strategy for HIART-MCS. • A theoretical model and schedulability analysis to provide a timing guarantee for the system, as well as a searching method to further optimise the mode switch strategy.

• Comprehensive experiments to examine HIART-MCS using different metrics. There have been existing work on theoretical model and analysis of IMCSs, e.g., [33]- [36] (see Sec. VIII). However, HIART-MCS is the first systematical solution for IMCS.

div.head: II. MOTIVATION: ENABLING IMPRECISION COMPUTATION
div.p: To enable imprecise computation, it is important to understand the working procedures of the processor when executing a task. Therefore, in this section, we first examine a 5-stage pipelined processor and then discuss the method used to enable imprecise computation.

div.head: A. 5-stage Pipelined Processor and Task Execution Time
div.p: Instructions are a processor's basic processing objects and a software task usually comprises hundreds and thousands of instructions. The best-known architecture of processor involves five essential stages in executing an instruction [37] (shown in Fig. 1):

• Instruction Fetch (IF): the processor fetches an instruction from its storage unit (e.g., instruction cache or SRAM) using an Instruction Fetch Unit (IFU). • Instruction Decode (ID): the processor decodes the instruction fetched by the IFU and then stores the decoded results in its local register files. • Execution (EX): the processor executes the instruction.

The processor contains multiple dedicated units for instruction execution. For instance, the Arithmetic Logical Unit (ALU) executes fixed-point calculations. • Memory Access (MA): the processor reads/writes data from/to its storage unit using a Load Store Unit (LSU). • Write-Back (WB): the processor writes the executed result back to its local register files for the next execution. As the essential execution phases of the processor, these five stages fundamentally determine the execution time of instructions and tasks. To quantitatively understand the relationship between these five stages and instruction execution time, we randomly generated 1, 000 instructions and then executed them independently using a RISC-V processor on our experimental platform (Xilinx VC709 [38], with the configurations discussed in Sec. VII). In the experiments, we connected a counter to the processor (driven by the same clock source as the processor) to measure and record the number of clock cycles taken by instruction executions at different stages. As shown in the experimental results (Fig. 2), the IF with cache hit, ID, and WB are usually completed in around one clock cycle,whereas the IF with cache miss and MA require slightly more clock cycles due to memory accesses. 1 An interesting result is observed at the EX stage: control instructions and fixed-point calculations usually require relatively fewer clock cycles for execution, whereas Floating-Point (FP) calculations use significantly more clock cycles in the execution, which dominates the execution time of the entire instruction.

div.head: B. Building IMCS using Approximation.
div.p: As the FP calculations in the EX stage consume significantly more clock cycles than the other execution stages, approximation, i.e., cutting down the valid bit-width of input operands, provides an opportunity to decrease such expensive consumption. Approximation accelerates the FP calculations from two folds: (i) skipping the calculations of the masked bits; (ii) increasing the hit rates of Trivial Calculation (TC). Based on the new processor, we configured the APU to mask the low 8/16 bits of the operands and then re-executed the experiments introduced in Sec. II-A. As shown in Fig. 2, with 8/16-bit approximation, the execution time of FP computations is reduced by 20/30% in average. This improvement is further magnified during TC-hit, where the processor always completes EX stage in a single clock cycle.

Generally, more operand bits being approximated leads to a higher degree of acceleration , which means a shorter task computation time and more computing imprecision. With this in mind, we designed an IMCS framework (HIART-MCS), which supports a new intermediate mode (MID-mode), that lies between LO and HI modes. In MID-mode, HIART-MCS executes LO-tasks using approximation, increasing the resilience of the system to temporary overloads and minimising the termination of tasks.

div.head: C. Research Challenges
div.p: Given the previously detailed concepts, it is possible to build a resilient and approximated computing architecture for IMCS. However, establishing a practical IMCS framework is not straightforward as several key challenges must be addressed:

• Before run-time, a qualitative analysis is required to determine the appropriate degree of imprecision of each LO-task and the associated impacts, including the task execution time and potential safety risks. • At run-time, a timely method is needed to configure the degree of imprecision of execution at task switches, as the tasks usually accept different levels of imprecision. • A systematic solution, including hardware and software implementation, to realise the new features introduced by IMCS is still missing. Context. In this paper, we assume (i) The platform is an embedded Network-on-Chip (NoC). Although HIART-MCS is agnostic to the types of interconnect, deployment of a NoC can enhance the predictability of on-chip transactions [39]. (ii) HIART-MCS is applicable to both single-and many-core architectures. A fully-partitioned scheme is adopted in a multi-/many-core system. Existing task allocation heuristics [1] (e.g., first-fit) can be applied directly for partitioning.

div.head: III. HIART -PROCESSOR
div.p: From the perspective of embedded/computer architecture, task execution involves system components at different levels, e.g., compiler, operating system (OS), etc. Therefore, it is possible to deploy approximation at any system level [40], [41]. In HIART-MCS, we selected the hardware processor level for approximation, due to the two-fold benefits:

• Compatibility: software tasks designed for conventional processors can be directly applied to the new processor, as the appximation is transparent to the tasks. • Supporting run-time data: different from approximation at other levels (e.g., at compiler level), the hardware-level approximation does not require input data to be known before run-time. In this section, we first study the FP formats used by the FPU, and then introduce HIART-MCS's FPU design.

div.head: A. Floating-Point (FP) Formats
div.p: The FP format defines the internal representation of FP numbers in the hardware. IEEE 754-2019 [42] regulates the data format of an FP number f , as defined in Eq. ( 2), where S is the sign, E is the exponent, and M is the mantissa (f = 0 is a special case, represented by setting both E and M to 0). formats use the highest bit as the sign presentation, but use different widths for the exponent and mantissa. The concept, design and analysis presented in this paper are agnostic to data widths. Following most de-facto embedded systems, we use a 32-bit FP format as an example throughout the paper.

div.head: B. FPU design in HIART-MCS
div.p: In Fig. 4, we illustrate the top-level design of the FPU in HIART-MCS (namely HIART-FPU), comprising a conventional FPU (C-FPU), a TCU and an APU, described below.
• C-FPU 2 -executes FP calculations if TC-miss;
• TCU -executes FP calculations if TC-hit;

• APU -controls the approximation degree of input data. During an FP calculation, two operands (filtered by the APU) and one operator are first transmitted to the TCU. The TCU checks whether the calculation matches a trivial case: if the calculation hits a trivial case, the TCU directly returns the calculation results based on Table I. Otherwise, the TCU generates a TC-miss signal to the C-FPU, which tells the C-FPU to proceed with the corresponding FP calculation. TCU design (Fig. 5). We designed the TCU using pure combinational logic, which ensures the TCU always completes each computation in a single clock cycle.

The TCU design comprises four Trivial Computation Machines (TCMs) and control circuits. The TCMs manage the trivial computations for addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division. The control circuits route the input operands to the TCMs and select the corresponding TCU output results based on the operator value. In each TCM, we present a number of sub-TCMs, with each sub-TCM checking a trivial case listed in Table I. All sub-TCMs have unified interfaces, with two input ports passing operands and two output ports returning the calculated results and the TC-hit status, respectively. We designed the APU to manage the degree of approximation of the operand mantissa bits and bypass the operator and operand sign and exponent bits from the APU. The APU design comprises two registers: an 8-bit configuration register stores the approximation degree configured by the software and a 23-bit mask register to control the valid bits of the operand mantissas. Note, in the configuration register, 0 indicates the lowest approximation degree, i.e., operands are not masked.

We connect the configuration register to an AMBA APB interface and map it to a dedicated memory address [43]. This allows the software to access the configuration register directly using memory write operations. Algo. 1 shows the software driver for the APU configuration. We also designed combinational circuits to convert the configuration register value to the corresponding mask register value. For instance, 0x08 in the configuration register is converted to 0x7FFF00 in the mask register. Finally, each bit in the mask register is connected to the corresponding operand bits using and gates, which filter the omitted bits required by approximation, i.e., the low 8 bits of the operands in the above example.

div.head: IV. TASKS IN MID-MODE
div.p: In the previous section, we discussed the design of a processor to support run-time configuration of approximation. To achieve the new MID-mode, we still need to determine (i) a task's applicability for approximation; (ii) the approximation degree of each approximatable task. This section discusses these two questions.

div.head: A. Applicability
div.p: Since approximation leads to inaccurate computation, it is only suitable for tasks with a certain level of error-tolerance. In an MCS, most HI-tasks are usually life-critical (e.g., engine control) and often require absolute computation accuracy (e.g., cryptography). Hence, we always execute HI-tasks with full precision and only consider approximation for LO-tasks.

To apply approximation in HIART-MCS, the LO-tasks must satisfy the following characteristics (C.x): C.1. The LO-tasks must contain FP computations, e.g., image processing [44], [45], signal processing [46], [47], machine learning [30], [48], etc. 3 , since HIART-MCS does not accelerate fixed-point computations. C.2. The LO-tasks must allow a trade-offs between computation precision and performance. C.3. With the specified approximation degree, the LO-tasks must maintain the correctness of computation within an acceptable range -higher 90% as a common criterion [40].
In the following section, we describe a method for finding a suitable degree of imprecision for LO-tasks at MID-mode.

div.head: B. Achieving new tuples for MID-mode
div.p: Executing LO-tasks in MID-mode requires two more features for each LO-task (denoted τ i ), which must be acquired offline:
• Approximation degree (denoted by M i ). When τ i executes in MID-mode, the APU masks M i bits of the operands' mantissas, where
div.formula: M i ∈ [0, 23]. • WCET in MID-mode (denoted by C AP i ).
div.p: Enabling approximation of τ i accelerates its execution, reducing τ i 's WCET from C LO i (in LO-mode) to C AP i (in MID-mode). Similar to the other tuples in the system (described in Sec. VI), these two new features can be obtained using either static analysis or experimental measurements. Considering the features of MCS and LO-tasks [1], in this paper, we adopted 3 These categories are not mutually exclusive. a measurement-based method (shown on the left of Fig. 7) to determine the new tuples, which is briefly introduced below:

Step 1: Initialisation and input generation. We initialise a conventional MCS and HIART-MCS using the examined task τ i . We randomly generate N input data for τ i , e.g., from the MNIST dataset for CNN tasks, 1, 000 times.

Step 2: Experimental measures. We first execute τ i with the generated input data using the conventional MCS and use the outputs as reference results. We then linearly tune HIART-MCS's M i from 0 to 23, and execute τ i with all input data under each system configuration. For each execution, we record the output results and the task execution times.

Step 3: Results analysis. We analyse the HIART-MCS output results and task execution times for each M i . Firstly, we compare the recorded τ i 's execution time and determine the maximum value as C AP i . Secondly, we deliver HIART-MCS's output results and reference results to an acceptance test function. The acceptance test function compares the two categories of results and returns a 'yes/no' label for each comparison to indicate whether the output result is in the acceptable range. Finally, we introduce a scoreboard to accumulate the 'yes/no' labels and calculate the QoC) using Eq. ( 3). If QoC > 90%, we consider the M i can be used by τ i in MID-mode.

div.p: Note, the design of the acceptance test function should be specific for each application domain. For instance, for CNN tasks, the acceptance test function only returns a 'yes' label when HIART-MCS's output result exactly matches the reference result; for image processing tasks, the acceptance test function returns a 'yes' label when the peak signal-tonoise ratio between the two results is less than 30db [41].

Following the experiments, the QoC and WCET of τ i under different approximation degrees (M i s) are plotted. Based on the results, the system designer is then able to determine the largest M i satisfying the approximation criterion, and the corresponding WCET (C AP i ). Example of a CNN task. The task was built on LeNet-5 architecture [50] and trained using the MNIST training dataset [51]. We chose 19 as the M i for the examined task in MID-mode, and its corresponding C AP i was equal to 62.7% of C LO i , as M i = 19 is the largest case ensuring QoC> 90%.

div.head: V. HIART -MCS: SYSTEM-LEVEL DESIGN
div.p: In the context of conventional dual-mode MCS theory, many practical frameworks have been proposed. For instance, Richard et al. [25], Gadepalli et al. [26], and Kim et al. [27]. To ensure compatibility with the state-of-the-art, we designed HIART-MCS based on conventional MCS frameworks. In this section, we summarise traditional MCS architecture in Sec. V-A and then present HIART-MCS's system-level design in Sec. V-B.

div.head: A. Conventional MCS Framework
div.p: The generalised system architecture of a conventional MCS (shown in the upper part of Fig. 8) is illustrated by considering a conventional embedded/computer architecture with Algorithm 2: Context switch and mode switch. Two essential functionalities must be supported by the execution monitor: (i) monitoring task execution times; and (ii) triggering a mode switch when detecting the over-execution of a HI-task. These functionalities are achieved using co-operation between a dedicated timer in the hardware and an additional library in the OS kernel (named MCS.mode switch). The execution monitor and introduced library are usually implemented either in the OS kernel (e.g., Kim et al. [27]) or in an independent hypervisor (e.g., Richard et al. [25]). Run-time behaviours. At system initialisation, the LO- WCETs of HI-tasks are preloaded to memory. During context switches, the execution monitor suspends the timer of the currently executing task and then (re-)activates the timer for the next executing task. If a HI-task runs over its LO-WCET, an interrupt sent from the hardware timer will trigger the execution of Lib.mode switch for mode switch. The pseudocode demonstrating this procedure is shown in the black text in Algo. 2 (the text in blue shows the additions in HIART-MCS).

div.head: B. HIART-MCS Framework
div.p: HIART-MCS brings changes to mode switch strategy, system architecture and run-time behaviour compared to a conventional MCS, which we now discuss. Mode switch strategy. The switching of criticality modes follows these steps (see Fig. 9):

(i) HIART-MCS initialises in LO-mode and stays in this mode if none of the HI-tasks exceeds their LO-WCETs, i.e., C i < C LO i ; (ii) When a HI-task τ i overruns its LO-WCET, i.e., C i > C LO i , at the instance of over-execution, the HIART-MCS immediately switches to MID-mode. In this mode, the LO-tasks can still be executed with approximated computation on, in which case their execution times should be less than an upper-bound, C AP i ; (iii) If the HI-task continues to overrun and exceeds a specific time point, HIART-MCS immediately switches to HI- mode while all LO-tasks are dropped. The time point triggering mode switch from MID-mode to HI-mode is termed MID-WCET (denoted as C MI i ). A method to obtain the MID-WCET is given in Sec. VI-C. System architecture. In the hardware layer, we replaced the processor (in conventional MCS frameworks) with the new HIART-processor. Since HIART-MCS needs to monitor HI- tasks' over-execution at two time points, i.e., LO-WCET and MID-WCET, we also introduced two hardware timers.

In the software layer, we modified the implementation of both the Lib.mode switch and the execution monitor. For the Lib.mode switch, we introduced a control function (Algo. 1) to manage approximation degree of LO-tasks in MID-mode. For the execution monitor, we controlled both hardware timers during context switches and updated mode switch strategy. Run-time behaviours. At system initialisation, the degrees of approximation of LO-tasks, as well as LO-WCETs and MID-WCETs of HI-task are preloaded (Algo. 2: lines 1 -3). During context switches, the execution monitor suspends the timers of the currently executing task and then (re-)activates the timers for the next executing task to monitor the over-execution of LO-WCETs and MID-WCETs, respectively (Algo. 2: lines 10 -11). If a HI-task exceeds its LO/MID-WCET, the corresponding timer generates an interrupt to trigger a mode switch (to MID/HI-mode) by invoking Lib.mode switch (Algo. 2: lines 32 -38). Note, the system also configures the degree of approximation of LO-tasks during context switch when the system executes in MID-mode (Algo. 2: lines 21 -25). Note that, with the increase of tasks, more timestamps are required to be kept in the memory, which will increase the memory size and affect the scalability of HIART-MCS.

Compatibility. Although the HIART-MCS introduces a new system architecture, the design minimises modifications to the software (shown in Algo. 2). Moreover, the design maintains the original OS-application interfaces presented by a traditional MCS (shown in Fig. 8). Therefore, user applications designed for a conventional MCS frameworks can be directly mapped to the HIART-MCS.
This section discussed HIART-MCS's system architecture, in the next section, we examine the benefits of the HIART-MCS theoretical model.

div.head: VI. TASK MODEL AND RESPONSE TIME ANALYSIS
div.p: Based on the system framework introduced above, we discuss a new scheduling strategy using approximate computing. In terms of task model, we use a standard dualmode (LO-mode and HI-mode) mixed-criticality model, with an additional transition mode (known as intermediate mode, or MID-mode) for handling temporal overloads. The objective of the additional mode is to: (i) reduce the number of mode switches to HI-mode; and, (ii) improve the number of surviving LO-tasks by reducing their QoC. Note that the system framework is generic, so the application is not limited to the model we discuss here. Also, in some applications, HI-task may also use approximate computing. However, these extensions are trivial and will not be discussed in this paper (detailed in Sec. IV-A).

div.head: A. System and Task Models
div.p: It is assumed that the system is scheduled with full partitioning, i.e., each partition has its own scheduler and can be scheduled and analysed independently. The local scheduler uses Fixed-Priority Preemptive Scheduling (FPPS). Within a partition, the system has a couple of tasks Γ = {Γ LO ∪ Γ HI }, where Γ LO is the set of LO-tasks, and Γ HI is the set of HI-tasks. A task is defined as a set of tuples:

div.head: B. Response Time Analysis
div.p: To check the schedulability for mixed-criticality systems [52] [53], two conditions need to be considered: (i) before/after mode switching; and (ii) during mode switching. One of the constraints of the HIART-MCS is that a task's M i (so is the C i ) cannot be changed during its execution. This is so as to not violate calculation consistency from approximation (so the result would not be from a mixture of half beforeapproximation and half after-approximation).

During the mode switch, the low-critical jobs that are currently running will discard that particular job instance. The dropping is only required at most one instance and the next job release will be executed normally with approximation on. Note it can be zero drop if the job instances have not started running when the switch happens. One can choose not dropping all (or some) of these jobs. However, this will result in reduced schedulability, as in the worst-case, these LO-tasks job instances will continue to run up to their C LO i , rather than what they should be in MID-mode, C AP i . This strategy improves survivability of LO-tasks against traditional AMC where all the following LO-tasks instances (rather than at most one) would be dropped [53].
Overall, we assume the following constraints to system:

• Constraint 1. A task which is currently running cannot turn approximation on, i.e., it uses its approximated execution time in the analysis; • Constraint 2. Overrun can only happen for HI-tasks if a LO-task overruns. This will be classed as an anomaly and is not discussed in this work. The HI-task can overrun up to C MI i in MID-mode and C HI i in HI-mode; To test the schedulability, both during-and post-transition phases should be checked.

Depending on the value of the execution time, the system will either switch from LO-mode to MID-mode, or from MID-mode to HI-mode. I. Switching from LO-Mode to MID-Mode: LO-tasks will run up to R LO i before MID-mode happens, once a HI-task overruns over C LO i ; HI-tasks can run up to C MI i . For HI-task, we have:
div.formula: Ri =C MI i + j∈hpH(i) Ri Tj C MI j + j∈hpL(i) R LO i Tj C LO j + j∈hpL(i) Ri -R LO i Tj C AP j (8
div.p: where R LO i /T j is the amount of interference before the mode switch where LO-tasks executes with C LO i . After R LO i , the execution time of LO-tasks becomes C AP i and can execute for another (R i -R LO i )/T j times. For LO-tasks: C i = C LO i ; while for HI-tasks: C i = C MI i . II. Switching from MID-Mode to HI-Mode: LO-tasks will be terminated (but may run up to R MI i ), in which case there is no R LO i , while HI-tasks can run up to C HI i . In this case, for HI-tasks we have:
div.formula: Ri =C HI i + τ j ∈hpH(i) Ri Tj C HI j + τ k ∈hpL(i) R MI i T k C AP k (9)
div.p: It is notable that it is also possible the HI-task would overrun up to C MI i immediately after it overruns C LO i , in which case (I) and (II) would happen within the same task instance and the system would benefit less from the MID-mode. In the above analysis, we assume all LO-tasks can run in MID-mode with approximate computing on. Alternatively, if this still does not meet schedulability, we can further drop some LO-tasks which are less important than the others. This, Algorithm 3: Finding the optimal value of gamma 1 Function searching_gamma(Γ, step): return γ; 18 End Function however, has to be checked against the safety requirements that the termination of these tasks would not compromise the system, which is beyond the scope of this paper and will be discussed in future work.

div.head: C. Solving C MI
div.p: i for HI-tasks Based on mode-switching, we can infer that a low C MI i will cause frequent unnecessary mode switches and should be avoided, while a high C MI i will challenge schedulability. We thus need to find a method, either heuristic or analytical, to calculate the optimal value of C MI i . In MID-mode, both HItasks and LO-tasks have to be schedulable.

The value of C MI i can be obtained through searching, subject to schedulability being satisfied. For search-based methods, we propose two approaches to calculate C MI i : (i) solving by priority ordering; and (ii) global scaling. I. Solving by priority ordering. Using RTA to iterate over all tasks from high-priority to low-priority, the search will start with the highest priority HI-task. The objective is to find the optimal C MI i by:
div.formula: C MI i = arg max C i (Rj ≤ Dj, ∀j ∈ Γ)(10)
div.p: where R j is calculated using RTA equations Eq. ( 4) - (9). Due to the way the algorithm executes, the highest priority HI-tasks will be searched first, as well as obtaining a more favoured C MI i . However, from the safety point of view, the probability of failure is not shown to be correlated with the priorities. This leads to the next search method. II. Solving by global scaling. In this case, the C MI i will be assigned more evenly across the HI-tasks. First, we define a global scaling factor γ:
div.formula: ∀i ∈ Γ HI , C MI i = C LO i + γ(C HI i -C LO i )(11)
div.p: To obtain gamma, we can solve using the following optimisation:
div.formula: γ * = arg max γ (Rj ≤ Dj, ∀j ∈ Γ)(12)
div.p: where R j is calculated using RTA equations Eq. ( 4) -( 9). Global scaling is preferred in cases where the failure model is not correlated with task priorities. In this case, all HI-tasks have an equal chance of overrun. Thus, the value of C MI i should be more evenly distributed. The γ search is done using a binary search, with a complexity of O(log(n)), compared to the linear search of O(n). The full algorithm is shown in Algo. 3. The schedulability test uses the response time equations to check the deadline of each HI-and LO-task, with the C MI i calculated using Eq. (11).

div.head: D. An Illustrative Example Taskset
div.p: Here, we give an example to illustrate the switching process and response time calculation. Consider the taskset given in Table III. The taskset is initially schedulable in LO-mode with all the tasks running up to C LO i . Assume now τ 1 overruns to 6 (C MI i ). A traditional dual-mode MCS system will switch to HI-mode, where τ 2 will be discarded, otherwise, τ 3 will not be schedulable. However, with MID-mode introduced, the HItasks will be executed under C MI i , while the LO-task can run with its MID-mode WCET (C AP i = 5). In this circumstance, the response time of τ 1 is unaffected as it is the highest priority task, and both τ 2 and τ 3 are now schedulable with R MI 2 = 17 < D 3 (25) and R MI 3 = 36 < D 3 (50). More results will be demonstrated through evaluation in Sec. VII-A.

div.head: VII. EVALUATION
div.p: Experimental platform. We built a 16-core HIART-MCS on a Xilinx VC709 evaluation board. We implemented the HIART-processors based on SiFive Freedom E31 [54], an open-source 32-bit RISC-V processor. Specifically, we enabled 5-stage pipeline of the processor (see Sec. II), and disabled multi-branch, out-of-order processing and related functionalities, e.g., branch prediction, as these functionalities are not related to this paper and may cause additional timing uncertainty. We implemented the required FPU and related modules (see Sec. III-B) using Verilog and integrated them into the processors. We connected the processors with memory and I/O peripherals using a 5 × 5 mesh type open-source NoC [39]. The software executing on the processors (OS kernels, drivers and user applications) was compiled using a RISC-V GNU tool-chain. We selected FreeRTOS (v.10.4) as the OS kernel for all processors, with the modifications introduced in Sec. V-B.

However, in the baseline systems (BSs), different variants are used in previous work. As reviewed in Sec. V-A, existing MCS frameworks usually implement run-time monitoring and mode switches either in OS kernels (OSK) [55] or a dedicated hypervisor (HYP) [56], [57]. Therefore, we built two BSs (BS-OSK and BS-HYP) on similar hardware platforms, using conventional RISC-V processors. BS-OSK is an MCS framework implementing execution monitoring and mode switches in OS kernels. BS-HYP is an MCS framework using virtualisation technology, including real-time patches and I/O enhancement [58]. BS-HYP implemented an execution monitor and mode switches in its hypervisor. All systems ran at 100 MHz.

div.head: A. Survivability of LO Tasks v.s. γ
div.p: In this experiment, we show the survivability of LO-tasks against the value of γ using theoretical evaluation, where the result is based on response time analysis on randomly generated tasks. Survivability in this context is the percentage of LO-tasks that can survive during overload, which is defined as:
div.formula: S = # of survived cases # of all cases × 100%(13)
div.p: Experimental Setup. The taskset used in the experiment is synthetically generated. The parameters used are described as follows: for each value of γ, 1000 trials were evaluated. Within each trial, one of the HI-tasks is randomally selected and is set to overrun and a schedulability test is applied to check whether the system is schedulable or not. The total utilisation of the taskset was set from 0.5 to 0.95, with an incremental step of 0.05. The task utilisations were generated using UUniFast. The taskset was schedulable in LO-mode (but not guaranteed for HI-mode). For LO-tasks: C AP i = 0.7 × C LO i , and for HI-tasks:
div.formula: C HI i = 3× C LO i .
div.p: Half of the tasks in the taskset were randomly selected as the HI-task. One of the HI-tasks was randomly selected to overrun to trigger a mode switch, with execution time uniformly distributed from C LO i to C HI i . The settings provide patterns close to practical applications and facilitate behaviour observation.

In the first part of experiment, we scaled the value of γ against survivability defined in Eq. (13). We counted the number of surviving tasks in both the dual-mode model and our tri-mode model, as well as counting the cases that survived using our model, but not in the dual-mode model. The results are shown in Fig. 10.

In the second part of the experiment, we explored the schedulability of the proposed tri-mode model against the traditional dual-mode MCS model (without MID-mode). Similarly, we randomly generated tasksets with total utilisation from 0.1 to 0.9 with a step of 0.05. Within each trial, we randomly selected one HI-task to overrun, similar to the first part of the experiment. The parameters of the proposed method were found through optimised searching of globally scaled γ (using the searching method discussed in Sec. VI-C). Obs 1. The proposed MCS model outperforms the traditional dual-mode model in terms of survivability and schedulability.

From the results of the first experiment (Fig. 10), it can be seen that there is a maximum 16% benefit of LO-tasks over the dual-mode model. It is also notable that with a higher Fig. 10. Survivability against total utilisation and the value of γ Fig. 11. Schedulability with and without the MID-mode utilisation, the proposed method works better compared to the traditional dual-mode model. This is confirmed in the second experiment (shown in Fig. 11), where the schedulability of the taskset with and without the MID-mode are shown; it can be seen that the difference between the two models increases with higher utilisation.

Note that the schedulability of the whole system is unchanged after the system has moved to HI-mode. However, the improved schedulability from MID-mode to before HI-mode can be used to fit more LO-critical tasks or prolong the survival time of LO-tasks.

div.head: B. Software Overhead
div.p: In this section, we compare the software overhead of a legacy system, 6 with BS-OSK, BS-HYP, and HIART-MCS. Experimental Setup. The software overhead was evaluated using the run-time memory footprint, with specific consideration of the OS kernel and execution monitor (memory size tool: RISC-V GNU tool-chain). The native OS kernel was fully-featured with essential I/O drivers [59]. Obs 2. HIART-MCS required less memory footprint than BS-HYP. Its software overhead was similar to BS-OSK.

This observation is shown in Fig. 12. HIART-MCS consumed significantly less memory footprint compared to BS-HYP (89kB, 32.6%). Due to the introduction of the execution monitor and the modifications to the OS kernel (detailed in Sec. V), HIART-MCS required an additional 41kB (27.0%) memory footprint compared to the legacy system. The overhead of HIART-MCS was similar to BS-OSK (109.7%).

div.head: C. Hardware Overhead
div.p: HIART-MCS required additional hardware implementation for its processor. We now evaluate the hardware overhead. Experimental Setup. We first configured HIART-processor to support run-time approximation of 100 tasks and compared this with a conventional RISC-V processor (Freedom E310). We also examined the HIART-processor's overhead along with other hardware elements in the system, including an AXI interconnect (AXI-IC) and two mainstream I/O controllers (SPI and Ethernet), which evaluated HIART-MCS's overhead from a system perspective. The AXI-IC and the I/O controllers were chosen from the standard Xilinx IP library with default settings. All components were synthesised and implemented by Vivado (v2020.2) [60] and compared using Look-Up-Tables (LUTs), registers, DSPs, RAMs and power. Obs 3. The design of the HIART-processor was resourceefficient compared to a generic processor. The introduced overhead was also less than the basic system elements.

As shown in Table IV, implementing the HIART-processor based on a RISC-V processor only introduced an additional 336 (6.7%) LUTs, 421 (7.9%) registers and 7 (1.9%) mW. This hardware overhead was significantly less than the other examined hardware elements: AXI-IC (39.8% LUTs, 53.5% registers, 45.5% mW), SPI controller (31.1% LUTs, 75.6% registers, 71.4% mW), and Ethernet controller (15.1% LUTs, 43.2% registers, 38.5% mW). Moreover, the implementation of the HIART-processor did not require any DSP or RAM.
In summary, Obs. 2 and 3 demonstrate that the HIART-MCS design is resource-efficient for both software and hardware.

div.head: D. Case Study
div.p: We configured all examined systems (including a legacy system) with 4/8/16 processors, and executed real-world use cases on each of them.
Task sets. We introduced three sets of real-world tasks:

• 18 HI-tasks, selected from Renesas functional safety automotive use case database [61], (e.g., CRC and RSA32). • 18 LO-tasks, including 6 DNN tasks, 6 image processing tasks, and 6 automotive function tasks selected from EEMBC [62] benchmark. The DNN and image processing tasks support approximation in MID-mode.

In the LO-task category, the DNN tasks were classified into two groups, built on LeNet-5 [50] and SqueezeNet (a variant of AlexNet) [63] architectures, respectively. In each group, the tasks were trained using MNIST, EMNIST and CIFAR-10 training datasets, respectively. The image processing tasks were designed to use Sobel filter, Canny filter, Scharr filter, Prewitt filter, Roberts filter and Sharpen filter for Oxford-IIIT Pet Dataset [64].

We employed a hybrid-measurement approach [65] to obtain measured WCETs for all tasks (C LO i ), and used the method introduced in Sec. IV-B to obtain LO-task experimental measurements, i.e., M i and C AP i . The HI-tasks had been certified as ASIL-D tasks [8], with analysed WCETs (C HI i ). We obtained the HI-tasks' C MI i using the method described in Sec. VI-C. Each task had a defined period, with initial system utilisation approximately 45%. Following Sec. VI, we adopted implicit deadlines for all tasks.

Synthetic workloads. We also introduced synthetic workloads, which can be optionally added into the system to control overall utilisation in the experiments. Like other LO-tasks, the synthetic workloads were also selected from the EEMBC automotive benchmark [62]. Notably, in practice, the execution time of a task is affected by diverse factors (e.g., cache miss rate); hence, adding synthetic workloads to a system only gives the system a target utilisation.

Experimental setup. We introduced three groups of experimental setups, which activated 4/8/16 processors to execute the experimental task sets and synthetic workloads. The raw data for processing by the tasks was generated off-chip and sent to the evaluated systems via two Ethernet controllers (1 Gbps) at run-time. The experimental results were stored in dedicated DRAMs. In each experimental group, we executed the examined systems 500 times under varying target utilisation from 45% to 100% (at intervals of 5% increments). Each execution lasted 500 seconds. For fair comparison, we also ensured the data input to the examined systems was identical in each execution.

Experimental metrics. We used two metrics to evaluate the examined systems under each target utilisation, success ratio and number of services (NoS). The success ratio recorded the percentage of an examined trail executed without deadline miss of any HI-task, and the NoS measured the number of LO-tasks executions.

Since HIART-MCS introduced inaccurate computation, it may cause faults during its execution (see Sec. IV). Therefore, we also examined HIART-MCS using system-level QoC to record the percentage of correct execution. 7 Obs 4. For HI-tasks, HIART-MCS ensured similar success ratios compared to conventional MCS frameworks. This observation is shown in Fig. 13(a). When the systems were configured with the same number of processors, HIART-MCS usually had slightly lower success ratios of HI- tasks compared to BS-OSK. This is because HIART-MCS is designed based on BS-OSK (see Fig. V), but executes more tasks in a specific time period (i.e., MID-mode), increasing the processors' workload pressure. Obs 5. For LO-tasks, HIART-MCS significantly increased throughput and decreased experimental variances compared to conventional MCS frameworks.

As shown in Fig. 13(b), compared to BS-OSK and BS-HYP, HIART-MCS increased LO-tasks' NoS by 34.3/ 45.5/ 52.7% and 64.4/ 94.5/ 106.2% in 4/8/16-core systems, respectively. Such improvements benefited from MID-mode in HIART-MCS, which effectively extended the "life cycles" of LO-tasks. At the same time, we also report that HIART-MCS achieved the lowest experimental variance in the examined systems, since introducing approximation in HIART-MCS increased the possibility of TC-hits and a TC-hit computation is always completed in a single clock cycle. Obs 6. HIART-MCS slightly decreased system-level average correctness ratios by about 1%.

This observation is shown in Fig. 13(c). Although we configured the QoC of the DNN and image processing tasks (in MID-mode) at about 90% (see Sec. IV-B), HIART-MCS still maintained the system-level QoC at around 99%. This is because the approximation does not affect the execution of HI- tasks and synthetic workloads, which mitigated the potential faulty results caused by the LO-tasks. Based on Obs. 4, 5, and 6, we conclude that HIART-MCS significantly increases LO-task throughput without obviously affecting HI-task execution. This conclusion is aligned with the results of the theoretical evaluation, Obs 1.

div.head: VIII. RELATED WORK
div.p: Imprecise MCS. In MCSs, a range of research efforts aiming to extend the "life-cycles" of LO-tasks have been presented. Burns et al. [28] and Baruah et al. [29] allocated certain time budgets to the LO-tasks at HI-mode, allowing the LO-tasks to be executed when HI-tasks are idle. This method provides an opportunity for LO-tasks to be executed at the HI-mode, 7 A correct execution means that the calculated result of a task release passes the corresponding acceptance test in Sec. IV. but it can only ensure the execution of certain LO-tasks, e.g., the LO-tasks with a relatively higher priority. Liu et al. [34], [66] proposed a theoretical model, which executes the LO- tasks at HI-mode with assumed imprecise computing. Associated with that, they also presented schedulability analysis to bound the worst-case behaviours of the theoretical model. Pathan et al. [35] and Huang et al. [33] further extended the IMCS model and analysis for many-core platforms. The work verified the possibility of applying imprecise computing in MCS. However, all the work solely focused on the theoretical perspective; a systematical solution is not presented. Hardware-level approximation. There has been existing work achieving hardware-level approximation using different methods. Kahng et al. [67] presented the design of an imprecise adder. Specifically, they split an N -bit adder to (N/k -1) sub-adders and removed the carry chain to reduce criticalpath delay, effectively improving the adder's performance and energy-efficiency. Similarly, Kulkarni et al. [68] introduced an imprecise multiplier and further enhanced their design to detect the error magnitude for error-intolerant tasks. Ma et al. [69], [70] proposed an imprecise FPU to accelerates the execution of DNN tasks. As demonstrated in the evaluation, the proposed FPU effectively reduces overall energy consumption compared to running the same DNN task using a traditional FPU. Moreover, Ndour et al. [71] and Felzmann et al. [72] introduced different methods to apply the imprecise computation units in a mature processor (i.e., RISC-V). However, the existing work was usually presented to improve the system throughput and energy-efficiency. It does not consider the realtime requirements in MCS, which hence cannot be directly applied in the context of MCS.

div.head: IX. CONCLUSION
div.p: In this paper, a novel MCS framework (HIART-MCS) supporting hardware-level approximation is proposed. With hardware assistance, HIART-MCS introduces an intermediate mode, which executes LO-tasks with imprecise computation instead of dropping them directly. The HIART-MCS system architecture, including a new mode switch strategy and design methods, is detailed. A new theoretical model and schedulability analysis are also presented to provide a timing guarantee for HIART-MCS, followed by optimisations of the mode switch strategy. As shown in the theoretical and practical evaluations, HIART-MCS effectively improves LO-task survivability with negligible impact on HI-tasks. In addition, HIART-MCS is resource-efficient.
